title: Lead and direct work teams, at

lessons.title: Planning and organising the team's work
lessons.html:
Planning and organising the team's work

This practical module is about leading a team on a poultry unit day after day: planning the work, directing people, keeping standards and building a reliable team.

Planning by flock cycle

Poultry work follows the flock cycle. Use the placement and depletion schedule to plan ahead:

  • Before placement: clean-out, washing, disinfection, maintenance, litter, pre-heating, equipment checks.
  • Brooding: intensive checks, heater and ventilation adjustments, crop checks, early mortality.
  • Growing or laying: daily routines, weighing, vaccination days, equipment raising, egg collection and grading.
  • Depletion: feed withdrawal timing, catching crew coordination, transport.

Rosters

Birds need care every day, including weekends and public holidays. Draw up rosters that cover all houses and shifts, comply with working hour and rest rules, rotate weekend duty fairly and are published in advance. Plan cover for leave and sickness so that no house is left unattended.

Allocating people

  • Use a skills matrix to match workers to houses and tasks.
  • Keep workers on the same houses where possible so they know their flocks.
  • Allocate vaccination, brooding and controller adjustments only to trained people.
  • Build allocations around biosecurity: no movement from older or sick flocks to young chicks on the same day where farm rules forbid it.
  • Pair new workers with experienced ones.

Resources

Check that the team has what it needs: PPE, cleaning materials, disinfectant, vaccines, record cards, tools, working scales, generator fuel. Order before stocks run out.

Daily plan

Write a simple daily plan for each shift: houses, routine tasks, special tasks, who does what, and deadlines. Display it in the office or share it with team leaders.

lessons.title: Directing work and maintaining standards
lessons.html:
Directing work and maintaining standards

Shift briefing

Start every shift with a short briefing: the plan, special tasks, issues from the previous shift, biosecurity and safety points. Keep it short and practical and invite questions.

Standard operating procedures

Key tasks need written standard operating procedures (SOPs): house entry, house walks, dead bird handling, water vaccination, weighing, clean-out, egg collection and power failure response. Train workers on the SOPs and check that they follow them.

Supervising during the shift

  • Walk the houses yourself; see the birds and the work, not only the records.
  • Check records for completeness and accuracy while workers are still on site.
  • Check biosecurity compliance: foot bath strength, clothing, hand sanitising, doors closed.
  • Check quality: litter condition, feeder and drinker heights, egg handling, cleaning standard.
  • Correct problems on the spot and explain why.

Handling problems

When a worker reports a problem - high mortality, low water use, equipment failure - act quickly: check, decide, involve maintenance or the manager as needed, and inform the team of the outcome. For suspected controlled diseases, escalate immediately so the manager can notify the state vet.

Safety leadership

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, the team leader must ensure safe work: PPE for dust, ammonia and chemicals; guards on fans and augers; lock-out before repairs; safe lifting; safe ladders. Stop unsafe work. Investigate injuries and near misses and fix causes.

Coordinating with others

Coordinate with the hatchery on chick deliveries, the feed mill on deliveries, the vet on visits, maintenance on repairs and catching crews on depletion. Make sure all visitors follow biosecurity.

Communication between shifts

Use a handover book or app to record what happened, what is outstanding and what needs attention on the next shift.

lessons.title: Developing and motivating the team
lessons.html:
Developing and motivating the team

Setting goals

Set team goals linked to flock performance and standards: mortality below target, weights on standard, records complete, biosecurity audits passed, zero lost-time injuries. Share progress weekly. People work harder for goals they understand.

Training

Keep a training plan from the skills matrix. Train using explain - demonstrate - practise - check. Train every new worker in biosecurity before they enter a house. Arrange formal training for safety-critical work such as generator operation, chemical handling and first aid. Record all training.

Feedback and recognition

  • Praise specific good work promptly and publicly.
  • Correct problems privately and calmly, focusing on the task.
  • Recognise good flock results as team achievements.
  • Use incentive schemes fairly where the farm has them.

Managing performance

When a worker does not meet standards, find out why: skill, tools, workload, personal problems or attitude. Coach and support first. Where there is misconduct, such as a deliberate biosecurity breach or theft, follow the farm's disciplinary code with HR. Keep records of feedback, training and incidents. Never discipline informally by shouting, threats or withholding pay.

Resolving conflict

Address disagreements early, listen to each side privately, focus on facts and agree solutions. Refer serious matters to management.

Wellbeing

Poultry work involves early hours, weekends, dust and sometimes distressing events such as mass culling during disease outbreaks. Watch for fatigue and stress, ensure proper breaks and facilities, and refer workers to support where needed.

Reviewing team performance

At the end of each flock, review results with the team: what went well, what problems occurred, what to change. Involving the team in reviews builds ownership and skills.

Key points

  • Plan work around the flock cycle and publish fair rosters in advance.
  • Allocate trained people to critical tasks and respect biosecurity in allocations.
  • Brief each shift, use SOPs and check work in the houses.
  • Lead safety and investigate incidents.
  • Set goals, train, recognise and review each flock with the team.

quiz.question: Why should rosters be published in advance and rotate weekend duty?

options.text: For fairness and so all houses are covered
Rosters are not needed on poultry farms
